pillar_reactions.evidence: Asked practical mechanics rather than pushing back: 'say you're at a hotel and they only have the dumbbells, what do clients typically like find a local gym with them with kettlebells or what do they usually do?' He then volunteered the one genuinely positive reaction of the call and tied it to himself: 'I do like the mobility thing. Cause I haven't been doing any mobility routines. I just jumped straight into the workouts. And I do think I probably need to add mobility component to it.'

The most questioned pillar, and all of it about whether the rules survive his actual life. Whether to train fasted or fed; whether specific ingredients are prohibited — 'like, for example, like, soy sauce'; how clients handle rice and bread being ingrained; and twice about eating out every meal in China and the pressure to stuff his face at family gatherings. He was answered with generalities and a deferral to Trevor's onboarding call each time — 'I don't want to go too specific with you because Trevor's going to look at everything' — so the questions were absorbed rather than resolved.

'Makes sense. Sweet.' No questions on the substance of the accountability mechanics — the weekly check-in, the direct phone access, the group calls. His only question in this section was about whether Trevor had ever coached two people living together, which was about his partner rather than about the pillar.

anchors.raw: it was like a YouTube coaching thing. Where it was a course to teach you how to like take your experience and monetize it through YouTube... I felt like I did the work, but like it kept feeling like the work I was producing wasn't like there was like one like one-on-one feedback, but it kept feeling like it never hit the mark.
anchors.competitor: An unnamed YouTube monetisation coaching programme, described as his most expensive purchase of this kind
anchors.note: The dominant anchor in the call and the one the whole close ran into. It is not a price anchor — it is a proof anchor. He has paid a comparable sum for one-on-one coaching, done the work, and got nothing, and he noticed that the visible successes were 'publicized as like the top students' while people at his level stalled. The rep's answer was the eight-kilogram guarantee, which he accepted intellectually and it changed nothing.

anchors.raw: Just, like, you know how, like, a six-pack has, like, six abs, and then the fourth... Has been more defined than I could say it has ever been. Granted, I had body fat covering it up, but even when I was skinny, it wasn't as built as it was, while also feeling like I am out of breath in just 5 or 10 minutes.
anchors.note: One week of free content had already produced a visible result he could point to, which is what convinced him the method works and simultaneously removes urgency from paying for it. The third call in the corpus where the anchor is a cheap or free substitute that genuinely works.

anchors.raw: The salary that we have as software developers, that's what we consider difficult money. Versus if we were to create an app that has passive income, that is considered not difficult money. And so I don't want to spend difficult money on this right now within a certain amount.
anchors.note: Not a competitor and not an affordability constraint — a self-imposed accounting rule about which money is permitted for which category of purchase. He confirmed he could pay cash. This is the anchor that actually decided the call and there is nothing in the playbook that addresses it. The rep's inversion of it was the best improvisation in the batch and still did not close.

anchors.raw: like a vacation to Thailand on the beach would not be as satisfying without abs
anchors.note: He benchmarked $6,000 against a luxury trip and concluded the coaching was the better purchase — 'that's a hard price range to buy just a random object of fun' and 'it's something that would actually make me happier'. The price itself was never contested; only the timing and the entitlement.

anchors.raw: I did buy previous courses before, uh, like I bought a calisthenics course. Um, it was like, uh, some amount of money per month. Um, but the, the workouts were just, there's so many things to do and it was hard to see progress.
anchors.note: A second failed paid programme, reinforcing the pattern that buying instruction has not previously worked for him. Both failures were on programme design and feedback quality, which is exactly what the one-on-one pitch claims to fix — the rep had the material to make that connection explicitly and did not.

unmet_demand.want: Coaching that also serves his partner, who lives with him, trains with him and has ankle issues — 'Has he ever coached, like, two people that live together?'
unmet_demand.why_unmet: The programme is priced and structured per individual: 'if your partner wanted to come in and do something... then we'd be looking at two investments for the coaching program.' There is no couples, household or second-seat option, and the rep resolved the gap by going off-policy rather than by offering a product — 'I'm technically not supposed to tell you this... if he's kind of following along with you, and he runs into a roadblock, just ask Trevor, he'll tell you.'

unmet_demand.want: A way to start now and pay as the money arrives, so a salaried lump sum is not drawn down before his venture produces revenue.
unmet_demand.why_unmet: Instalments exist but are not offered as a product. They surfaced only in the final two minutes, unpriced and unstructured — 'we can probably just split up the payments remaining' — and gated behind individual approval: 'I have to get confirmation from Trevor on every time we do that.' A prospect who had already said he could pay cash but would not, and who wanted a smaller first commitment, was carried through eighty-eight minutes before the option that addressed him was mentioned.

unmet_demand.want: Concrete guidance for eating out every meal while travelling in Asia, and for family gatherings where the norm is to keep eating. He raised it three separate times.
unmet_demand.why_unmet: Each time it was deferred to the onboarding call — 'I don't want to say too much now because Trevor's going to look at your lifestyle' — and answered in principle rather than with anything specific. The programme may well handle this well; nothing on the call demonstrated it, and it was the concern the prospect returned to most often.
